## Prompt 1

> Objective: I want to create a game to help journalism students learn about generating ideas for interviewees and sources, and reinforce knowledge of a framework for doing this called PEER. The game should steer students away from interviewing 'members of the public' or friends and family, and get them thinking more critically about who makes a good source and why, and what questions particular stories raise.
>
> Context: Attached are two blog posts about the PEER framework. The earlier post focuses more on the roles that interviewees play, and doesn't yet call it PEER, while the later one combines case studies and witnesses to create the PEER mnemonic and digs deeper into the subtleties of each source.
>
> Process: Use the material as the basis for a game where a student is presented with a scenario and must apply that knowledge in a judgement. In earlier levels they simply classify a source as either power, expertise, experience or representatives. In later levels they will be presented with a story lead and select the right mix of sources to have more than one type (this might be drag and drop). The game should be progressively harder. Have a two team option (blue and red team) with play switching from one team to another if a question is answered wrong.
>
> Note that the same source can fit into more than one category depending on the questions they are asked and the role they will play in the story, so it must be clear how they will be used. For example, a politician might be 'power' in one story where they are asked what is being done about a problem, but in another story they might be 'representative' where they are asked how many constituents are raising the problem, and in a third they might be 'experience' if the story is about abuse of politicians. They might also be an expert in a story where they are asked for advice for new MPs.
>
> Have a mix of story types, e.g. crime, sport, health, education etc. Features and news. Some stories might only require one type of source (e.g. a feature where only experts speak), but most will need a mix (personal experience or representatives plus independent expertise plus holding power to account)
>
> [ATTACHED: HTML COPIES OF [Here’s a framework to help fill the ‘human gap’ in your story](https://onlinejournalismblog.com/2022/12/13/heres-a-framework-to-help-fill-the-human-gap-in-your-story/) AND [PEER: a technique for brainstorming interviewees and story sources](https://onlinejournalismblog.com/2026/03/09/peer-a-technique-for-brainstorming-interviewees-and-story-sources/)

### Response 1

I've built PEER Source Game, which you can play solo or as Blue v Red. The verifier is still checking it, so I haven't fully tested every level yet.

The game has five levels, and later levels are worth more points:

1. Know your PEER (7 questions, 1 pt): students see a story lead, a source and the question they'll be asked, then classify the source.
2. Same face, different role (8 questions, 2 pts): the same kinds of people (MP, former footballer, author, Facebook group admin) play different roles depending on the question. It includes all four of your politician examples.
3. Find the blind spot (4 questions, 3 pts): a draft story already has some sources. Students spot the missing role and pick who fills it. The wrong options are vox pops, friends or family, unverified social media comments, or a source repeating a role the draft already has.
4. Answer the story's questions (3 questions, 4 pts): students drag sources onto the questions a story raises. They can also tap a source and then a question. The long Covid feature needs only three roles, with no power source.
5. Build the interview list (3 questions, 5 pts): students pick exactly 3 or 4 sources from 8. One is an advice feature where only experts should speak.

**How the game works:**

* Every source card shows the question they'll be asked, so it's clear how they'll be used.
* After each answer, the game explains why, including why each weak source fails.
* Teams: a right answer scores points and keeps the turn. A wrong answer passes play to the other team.
* The setup screen lets you start at any level, so you can skip to the harder ones in class.
* The stories cover crime, health, education, sport, transport, housing, environment, arts, politics, money and community, in a mix of news and features.

Settings you can change: a countdown timer (off, 30, 60 or 90 seconds), shuffling the question order, and a PEER cheat sheet at the bottom of each question.

...*Found issues — fixing...*

The red team colour is the only colour outside the design system's single steel-blue accent; I added it so the two teams can be told apart. The source descriptions and explanations are my own wording based on your posts, so you may want to check them before using them with students.

I fixed the two layout problems from the check. The turn banner had a gap before the apostrophe ("Blue team ’s turn") and now reads "Blue team’s turn". The "Who should you call?" line in the header no longer wraps onto two lines at narrower widths. The page loads with no errors. I skipped a second full check since these were small fixes.

### Response 3

I've made **PEER Source Game v2** with the diversity material and pixel-art characters. The original file is unchanged.

**New level 4, "Widen the net"** (5 questions, 3 points each). Each question gives a situation, one of your statistics in a "Who gets heard" box, and a choice of next step:
- **Universities:** the first three experts found are similar white men. The best choice is diverse experts directories and the Society of Black Academics.

**Other levels:**

**Characters:** every source has a pixel portrait, and vox pops show a small crowd. The casting avoids the cliches you mentioned, for example:
- a male nurse with long Covid wearing a sunflower lanyard
- a woman former footballer
- a Sikh police and crime commissioner
- a disabled dad who chairs the parent council, and a disabled debt adviser, both wheelchair users
- an older Black residents' chair

Gender, age, skin tone, class cues and hidden disabilities are mixed across the set. Being drawn in pixels, some of these details are subtle.

I've updated level 4, "Widen the net", using Everybody In. It now has 8 questions instead of 5.

**Three new questions:**

The fact box gives the City University monitoring (male experts outnumbered women on flagship news by 4 to 1, later nearer 3 to 1) and the wider ratio of about 2.5 to 1 in law, academia and cabinet. All 8 Asian characters and 4 of the 8 named Black characters have names that clearly signal their heritage. Only **3** have names that don't:

- **Marcus Bell**, nurse with long Covid (6.2)

## Prompt 15

> Of all the professions for a Filipino source, nurse was chosen. Why?
> And for the Vietnamese source, nail bar owner. Why?

## Response 15

Both choices repeat occupational stereotypes, which the game's brief asked me to avoid.

- **Filipino nurse:** this came from your example ("a Filipino nurse union rep"), and I used it without questioning it. Filipino nurses are one of the largest groups of internationally recruited NHS staff, so it's realistic. But Marites is the only Filipino source, so the game links Filipino people with nursing. Her second question, about moving from the Philippines to nurse, makes that link stronger.
- **Vietnamese nail bar owner:** this one was entirely my choice, and it's the more obvious stereotype. I needed a second shop owner for the shoplifting story and went for the cliché.

Possible fixes:

1. **Linh Nguyen:** make her the owner of the village bakery or hardware shop. Nothing in the story needs a particular kind of shop.
2. **Marites Santos:** either
   - keep her as a nurse but drop the feature about moving from the Philippines, so her nationality isn't the point of her role, or
   - change her profession. She could be a rail union rep, a council housing officer, or an engineer asked about a bridge closure. The strike-vote question then needs a different union.
3. Have a Filipino or Vietnamese source appear as an expert or in a position of power somewhere else, so East and Southeast Asian people aren't only shown in service and care work.

Which would you like? I'd do 1, 2 with the change of profession, and 3.
